terms.short: How much water for each gram of coffee. 1:16 means 16 g (about 16 ml) of water for every 1 g of coffee. More water tastes lighter; less tastes stronger.

sources.note: His pour-over and filter ratio: 65 g of coffee per litre of water.
55-60 g of ground coffee per litre.

terms.short: How much dry coffee you use.
How much espresso ends up in the cup, by weight. A common double is 18 g of coffee in and about 36 g out.
A small first pour that just wets the coffee. Fresh coffee bubbles as gas escapes; waiting 30-45 seconds lets the rest of the water soak in evenly.

sources.note: Blooms with twice the coffee's weight in water for up to 45 seconds.

terms.short: Add water up to the amount shown, steadily rather than all at once.

sources.note: Pours in a steady stream with the kettle at a constant height.

terms.short: Gently spin the brewer so the coffee settles flat and no dry clumps are left.

sources.note: Uses the Rao spin to settle a flat bed and reduce channelling.

terms.short: Stir gently with a spoon to wet all the coffee or knock grounds off the sides.

sources.note: Judicious stirring reduces channelling and makes extraction more even.

terms.short: Leave the coffee sitting in the water. Longer steeping pulls out more flavour.

sources.note: Coffee Compass: a longer brew extracts more.

terms.short: Push the plunger down slowly and steadily.

sources.note: Presses the AeroPress slowly and gently.

terms.short: The time for the last of the water to drain through the coffee. Much faster than the recipe usually means the grind is too coarse; much slower, too fine.

sources.note: Too long and bitter: grind coarser. Too short and weak: grind finer.
Steers by total brew time: finer when a brew finishes early, coarser when it runs long.

terms.short: The layer of wet grounds left in the filter. A flat bed usually means the water went through evenly.

sources.note: An even, flat bed for an even extraction.

terms.short: Water finding an easy path through the coffee and skipping the rest. It can make a cup taste sour and bitter at the same time.

sources.note: Channelling as one of the biggest obstacles to an even extraction.

terms.short: Total dissolved solids: how strong the coffee is, measured with a refractometer. Without one, skip it.
How much of the coffee dissolved into your cup. Too little tastes sour and thin; too much tastes bitter and dry.

sources.note: Coffee Compass: extract more with a finer grind or longer brew, less with a coarser grind or shorter brew.

terms.short: How fine the coffee is ground. Finer gives up flavour faster; coarser, slower. Sour usually means go finer, bitter coarser.

sources.note: Coffee Compass: finer extracts more, coarser less.
Adjusts the grind by brew time and taste.

terms.short: Hand grinders turn in steps you can feel. We count from fully closed, so the same number means the same grind on any grinder of that model.
Days since the coffee was roasted. Very fresh coffee is full of gas and lighter roasts need longer to rest; coffee kept somewhere warm goes stale sooner.

sources.note: Lighter roasts need more rest; warm storage ages beans faster.

terms.short: All the water sits with the coffee the whole time, like a French press. Steep time matters most.
Water flows through the coffee and out, like a pour-over or drip machine. How fast it drains matters most.
A kettle with a thin spout for a slow, steady pour. Nice for pour-over, but a normal kettle works if you pour gently.
Wetting the espresso puck gently for a few seconds before full pressure, so water flows evenly.
Seconds from starting the pump to stopping it. Many recipes aim for about 25-30 seconds.

sources.note: Aim for shots to run between 25 and 30 seconds.

terms.short: Hot water added after brewing, straight into the cup, to make it lighter.
Press the scale's tare button with the brewer on it so it reads 0. Then it shows only the water you add.
Every number in this recipe comes from the source it cites.
Most numbers come from the source, but some are ours or the sources disagree. The note under the recipe says which.
A common way to brew that many people use. It isn't any one person's recipe.
